fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes a nanocrystalline refractory bulk alloy with grain boundaries for the target sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, where free surfaces and particle shape govern behavior.
It predicts entropy-assisted stability and restricted segregation, opposite to the observed non-sluggish diffusion, Au/Cu surface segregation, melting, evaporation, and particle-size loss.

The cited evidence does not establish that grain boundaries act simultaneously as diffusion barriers and sinks that suppress segregation; grain boundaries can instead provide fast diffusion and segregation pathways.
The proposed above-1000 degrees C atmospheric treatment does not reconstruct the target vacuum heating sequence up to 973 K.
explanation: The response addresses high-temperature stability of a high-entropy material only at a broad thematic level. Its material system, processing route, relevant interfaces, temperature regime, and proposed governing mechanism differ fundamentally from the target. The target concerns surface-energy-driven segregation and evaporation in isolated multicomponent nanoparticles, whereas the generated hypothesis concerns grain-boundary-mediated stabilization in additively manufactured refractory nanocrystalline material. The nano-grained versus coarsened comparison is testable, but annealing used to create the two states can also change precipitates, residual stress, texture, and chemical homogeneity, so it does not uniquely isolate grain-boundary density. E1 supports thermal stability of one nanocrystalline refractory HEA under extreme environments but not the asserted sink/barrier mechanism; E2 supports manufacturability and is not evidence for thermal stabilization by grain boundaries.
